problem_statement: At the time a loan application is submitted, I use the 22 available features to estimate the risk of default within the next 90 days. In this lab, I use synthetic applications to compare how well three models rank that risk.

notes.evidence: I selected Logistic Regression because it had the highest ROC-AUC (0.821) on the 2,000 comparison applications. Its average precision was 0.326, only 0.008 below XGBoost's 0.334. Given that small gap, I prefer the simpler model as my starting point.
notes.limitation: One random split of synthetic applications cannot establish how well the model will perform on future applicants. The split also allows the same customer to appear in both development and comparison data.
notes.next_test: I would train on earlier applications whose 90-day outcomes were known at the training cutoff, then test on later applications from different customers. I would switch to XGBoost if it consistently achieved higher AP and found more defaults within the same review capacity.

exit_answers: Only 7.9% of the comparison applications resulted in default. ROC-AUC measures how often a default is ranked above a non-default. AP tells me how precise the model's flags are as it captures more defaults. The distinction matters here because the two metrics favor different models.

Early stopping uses the inner-stop labels to choose the number of trees. Using the comparison rows for that choice would let their outcomes influence the model and could make its score look too optimistic. Keeping them separate gives all three fitted models a fair comparison.
